lesson.title: Case Conversion: .upper() and .lower()
lesson.summary: The .upper() and .lower() string methods return new, case-converted copies of a string, making them the standard tool for normalizing text before comparison.
lesson.body:
Every string in Python already knows how to change its own capitalization, because .upper() and .lower() are methods built into the string type itself. Calling some_text.upper() returns a brand new string with every letter converted to uppercase, and some_text.lower() does the reverse, converting every letter to lowercase. This is the same dot notation you learned with String Methods generally: the method belongs to the string object, so you call it after the string with a period, and it hands back a result rather than changing anything silently in the background.

The real reason these two methods matter so much is normalization. Computers compare strings character by character, so the string "Cat" and the string "cat" are not equal as far as Python is concerned, even though a human reader knows they mean the same word. If you are checking whether a user typed "yes" to confirm an action, but they typed "Yes" or "YES" instead, a plain equality check like answer == "yes" will fail and reject a perfectly valid response. Converting both sides to the same case before comparing removes that whole category of bug.

Here is a worked trace. Suppose answer = "YES". Writing answer.lower() looks at each character: 'Y' becomes 'y', 'E' becomes 'e', 'S' becomes 's', producing the new string "yes". The variable answer itself is untouched, still holding "YES", because strings are immutable and methods that transform them return a new object instead of editing the original in place. If you want to keep the lowercase version, you must assign it: answer = answer.lower(). Skipping that assignment is one of the most common beginner mistakes with these methods, since it is easy to assume the method changes the string for you.

A practical pattern combines this with an input loop:

answer = input("Continue? (yes/no): ")
while answer.lower() not in ("yes", "no"):
    answer = input("Please type yes or no: ")
if answer.lower() == "yes":
    print("Continuing...")

Here answer.lower() is recomputed each time it is needed rather than stored once, which is fine for a short script, though in longer programs you might normalize once and reuse the result.

Python also provides .capitalize(), which uppercases only the first character and lowercases the rest, and .title(), which uppercases the first letter of every word. Trace .title() on "hello world": Python finds the start of each word, 'h' and 'w', capitalizes those two letters, and lowercases everything else, producing "Hello World". These build on the same idea but solve a different problem: display formatting rather than comparison. There is also .casefold(), a more aggressive version of .lower() meant for comparing text that might include non-English characters, though for ordinary English text .lower() is what you will use in practice.

Keep upper and lower in mind as your default tool whenever "does this text match, regardless of how it was typed" is the real question you are asking. Whenever you find yourself writing several if-statements to catch different capitalizations of the same word, that is a strong signal you should be normalizing the case once instead.
